newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Strikes add to S.Korea's ballooning deficit.
newsitem.headline: Strikes add to S.Korea's ballooning deficit.

text.p: Strikes crippling South Korean industry have fuelled a sharp year-end surge in the current account deficit, the central bank said, further knocking a fragile economy.
Industrial stoppages could help lift the deficit this year to more than $22 billion from an earlier forecast of $21.5 billion, the central bank said on Monday.

"Traditionally, we've seen strong exports at the end of the year. But that's unlikely to be the case this year with labour strikes hindering exports during the last week of this month," said central bank director Paeng Dong-joon.
"At this point, the current account deficit is seen well above $22 billion for the year."
The deficit for calendar 1995 was $8.95 billion.
The central Bank of Korea said the current account deficit expanded to $1.87 billion in November from $179.6 million a year earlier.
The deficit was $21.6 billion for the first 11 months of this year, compared with $8.6 billion a year ago.
Exports usually jump towards the end of the year as the government pushes for more exports to improve the trade balance for the whole year.
However, attempts to dress up the figures have failed dismally this year due to unexpected strikes by workers at South Korea's leading export industries, including carmaking and shipbuilding.
Workers have downed tools to protest against a new labour bill passed by the National Assembly last Thursday.

On Monday subway drivers returned to work and nurses prepared to back down, but militant union leaders said it was only a temporary retreat to avert chaos during the New Year holidays and industrial action would resume with new ferocity next year.
Figures issued by the government indicated the number of strikers was falling, although major shipyards and car plants were still idle.

"The strikes are expected to result in an exports loss of $200-300 million in December, widening the current account deficit for the whole year," said Lee Jeun-tae, an economist at LG Economic Research Institute.
He said the institute had revised the 1996 current account deficit projection to $23 billion from $22.6 billion following the strikes.
"If the strikes phase out in early January, it won't be too bad. But if they are extended, we are in trouble," Lee said.
Daewoo Economic Research Institute said the current account deficit could expand to $21.7 billion next year compared with a previous best-case estimate of $18.1 billion.
"A slowdown in automobile exports is expected to batter South Korea's current account the most," said Shin Hoo-shik, a senior economist at Daewoo Economic Research Institute.
"Shipbuilding losses will hurt exports to a lesser degree because they won't have such a direct and immediate impact."
The central bank attributed the widening deficit in November to a continuing exports slump and rising imports.

This year's plunge in 16-megabit dynamic random access memory (DRAM) prices by about 80 percent has been cited as the biggest single factor dampening exports. Semiconductors make up about 20 percent of exports.
